records.title: release(v5): resolve standards blockers before latest promotion
records.body:
# OpenWA v5 release-readiness — Standards review

Date: 2026-08-13  
Candidate: `407c97055a762d207b614d2ba45ee13ef1faa320` (`master`)  
Comparison: npm `latest` `@open-wa/wa-automate@4.76.0`  
Published prerelease checked: npm `alpha` `@open-wa/wa-automate@5.0.0-alpha.8`

## Decision

The candidate is not ready to become the public v5 `latest`. The stable publish path cannot currently put a stable release on `latest`; the public package graph omits new runtime packages from stable versioning; the candidate has no green, comprehensive qualification run; and important supply-chain, Docker, licensing, and release-control gates are incomplete.

**PROMOTE: no**

## Findings

### BLOCKER — The publish wrapper cannot promote a stable build to npm `latest`

Evidence:

- `.changeset/pre.json:2-3` is still in `"mode": "pre"` with tag `"alpha"`.
- `tools/release/publish-packages.sh:42-55` returns plain `publish` only while the pre-mode tag is `alpha`; for every non-pre-mode state it constructs `publish --tag alpha`.
- `.github/workflows/release.yml:92-103` has no stable/tag input or promotion-specific branch: every release calls the same wrapper.
- Every publish-related package manifest at the candidate is still `5.0.0-alpha.7`; the pending changesets are patch changes, not a reviewed stable-exit plan.
- Live registry verification showed `@open-wa/wa-automate` tags are correctly isolated today (`latest=4.76.0`, `alpha=5.0.0-alpha.8`), but the repository has no path that exits prerelease mode and publishes stable `5.0.0` without forcing `alpha` again.

Why this fails the standard: a successful workflow run after `changeset pre exit` would still explicitly publish under `alpha`, so it would not perform the requested public `latest` promotion.

Smallest corrective action: add an explicit, reviewed stable-release mode. Exit Changesets pre-mode in a dedicated version PR, make the publish wrapper omit `--tag` (or explicitly use `latest`) only for stable versions, fail if the requested tag and version prerelease status disagree, and dry-run the exact stable version/tag transition before publishing.

### BLOCKER — Five public runtime packages are outside the fixed/pre-release topology

Evidence:

- Read-only manifest comparison found 32 public workspaces but only 27 entries in `.changeset/config.json:10-39`.
- The five public omissions are `@open-wa/runtime-browser`, `@open-wa/runtime-bun`, `@open-wa/runtime-core`, `@open-wa/runtime-edge`, and `@open-wa/runtime-node`.
- The same five are absent from `.changeset/pre.json:4-43` initial versions.
- `packages/wa-automate/package.json:31-32` now has production dependencies on `@open-wa/runtime-core` and `@open-wa/runtime-node`; `packages/runtime-node/package.json:17-20` in turn depends on `@open-wa/runtime-core`.
- All five candidate manifests are `5.0.0-alpha.7`, and `npm view` returned `E404` for all five package names/versions. They were not part of the alpha.8 tag set either.
- `.changeset/README.md:18` and `tools/release/README.md:120-125` claim all `@open-wa/*` public packages share fixed versions, which is false for these workspaces.

Why this fails the standard: a stable version pass over the configured fixed group can produce stable packages that depend on separately versioned prerelease runtime packages. At best, Changesets may opportunistically publish the missing alpha versions; it cannot turn them into the same reviewed stable version under the current configuration.

Smallest corrective action: add all intended public runtime packages to the fixed group and stable-exit changeset/pre-state (or mark them private if they are not supported), then verify that every internal production dependency resolves to the exact stable release and that all 32 public packages install from a clean registry.

### BLOCKER — There is no green comprehensive qualification for this candidate

Evidence:

- The repository has only seven workflows. None runs the root `build`, `test`, `typecheck`, and `lint` baseline for all pull requests or all candidate changes. The specialized triggers in `.github/workflows/effect-contracts.yml:3-25`, `.github/workflows/docs-quality-gate.yml:6-12`, and `.github/workflows/v4-parity.yml:7-14` cover selected paths only.
- The release workflow installs dependencies and invokes Changesets (`.github/workflows/release.yml:34-103`). Its wrapper builds at `tools/release/publish-packages.sh:70-71`, but neither path runs the full test, typecheck, or lint baseline promised by `CONTRIBUTING.md:69-75`.
- GitHub reported no substantive test/build check on candidate `407c97055`; its only check runs were failed Dependabot update jobs. `master` has no required status checks and does not enforce administrators; `release` is unprotected and there are no repository rulesets.
- The newest Effect-contract push run on an ancestor of the candidate failed. The root command tests all runtime workspaces before building them (`package.json:27`), and run `30778096277` failed because runtime-browser/edge/bun could not resolve the unbuilt `@open-wa/runtime-core` entry. No later successful run covers the candidate.
- The local dry-run is not a gate: package publication failures are warnings (`tools/release/dry-run.sh:296-314`), clean-install failure is also only a warning (`tools/release/dry-run.sh:351-376`), and the script can complete successfully with failed/skipped packages.

Why this fails the standard: a direct push to the release branch can publish an unqualified candidate even while the only relevant runtime contract workflow is red. A build-only publish step is insufficient for a public major.

Smallest corrective action: add a required candidate workflow that runs frozen install, build, tests, typecheck, lint, package/tarball validation, clean-registry installation, CLI smoke, and Docker smoke on the exact release SHA. Fix the Effect job ordering (`build` dependencies before consumer tests), make dry-run failures fatal, protect `master` and `release`, and requir

records.title: Give a permission-grant finding a precise line again, from the parse rather than a text search
records.body:
Split out of #364, which ships without it.

## Why there is no line today

A structured-config finding (`.claude/settings.json`, `.mcp.json`, `.aider.conf.yml`) names the FILE and not a line. That is deliberate. `allow` and `deny` hold textually identical values — only the structure carries the polarity — so locating the offending entry by searching the raw text can return the DENY entry, and the finding then prints `Fix: replace "Read(**/*.key)"` against the rule that stops an agent reading private keys, directly under guidance promising deny entries are never reported.

Three attempts to make a text search structure-aware are recorded in `src/scanner/permission-vocabulary.ts`, each smaller and sharper than the last, each still wrong:

1. **Search from the grant key's line.** Beaten by an earlier *bounded* `allow` key, by a `// allow:` comment above the deny list, and by a JSON-escaped key.
2. **A containment guard** over indentation-enclosure plus the nearest key named to the left within a line. Closed all of the above, and was quadratic in line length (`detect` 52.5s on a 200KB config where the base is 0.29s, reachable through `secure`, which has no size cap), retained one array per line (fatal out-of-memory in `secure` on a 3.8MB settings file), and *still* cited a deny entry when an array element is indented less than its own key — plainly formatted JSON.
3. **Emit a line only when the document declares no restriction key at all.** The premise was about the FILE; the implementation could only answer for the first 13 levels of the PARSED object, while the text search it gated read the whole file with no depth bound. A `deny` nested deeper — or reached through a YAML alias that poisoned the visited set — put the citation back on the deny entry.

So the fourth attempt must not be a fourth text heuristic. The grant has to carry its own offset from the parse.

## Shape of the fix

- **JSON:** a position-tracking parse, or a scanner recording `{key, valueStart, line}` per node. `stripJsonComments` in `src/scanner/permission-grant.ts` already walks the document character by character respecting string literals, and is the natural place to grow one.
- **YAML:** `js-yaml` exposes no per-key positions through `load`. Its `listener` option gives `state.line`/`state.position` on open/close events and is the only in-library route; otherwise the YAML half cites the grant key's own line, which is honest even if less precise.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Complexity **measured**, not argued, on 200KB and 4MB configs, through **both** `detect` and `secure` — `secure` has no size cap and is the CI gate.
2. Memory bounded: no per-line or per-node retained allocation.
3. The generated-corpus property test keeps **entry indentation as a free axis** (a previous corpus varied seven axes, pinned that one, and was blind to 60% of its own hazard), and keeps the naive-locator control proving the corpus carries the hazard.
4. A source-level regex gate is not sufficient alone: the `AMBIGUOUS_PAIR` guard returns false for the pattern that caused attempt 2's quadratic, because that shape is not the `X* Y? X*` family. Any new pattern needs a direct timing probe.
5. Any bound the solution carries — depth, size, a visited set — must be answered by the **same mechanism** that produces the citation. Attempt 3 failed precisely because a bounded structural check gated an unbounded text search. If the parse bounds itself, the citation must be **absent** past that bound, never guessed.
6. Restore the `secure` side too. With no line, `CLAUDE-002` emits no `Verify:` at all (`generateVerifyCommand` needs a line, and `SecurityFinding` has no explicit verify field). `detect` substitutes `cat`; `secure` cannot, and the asymmetry is unintended.

## Verify the current behaviour

```
mkdir -p /tmp/cit/.claude && printf '%s\n' '{' '  "permissions": {' '    "allow": ["Read(src/**)"],' '    "deny": ["Read(**/*.key)"],' '    "extra": { "allow": ["Read(**/*.key)"] }' '  }' '}' > /tmp/cit/.claude/settings.json
node dist/cli.js detect /tmp/cit --ci | grep -E 'grant broad permissions' -A 1
# names .claude/settings.json with no ":line"; Verify is `cat`, not `sed -n`
npx vitest run __tests__/scanner/permission-grant.test.ts -t 'no structured config carries a line'
```

records.title: Add tests to detect incomplete dependency metadata in AIPCC packages
records.body:
## Problem

[AIPCC-9537](https://issues.redhat.com//browse/AIPCC-9537) revealed that AIPCC-repackaged Python packages can have stripped or incomplete dependency metadata compared to their upstream PyPI counterparts. The `kfp` 2.15.2 package in AIPCC 3.3 was missing declarations for:

- `docstring-parser`
- `click-option-group` (not even in AIPCC index)
- `google-api-core`
- `google-cloud-storage`
- `kfp-pipeline-spec`
- `kfp-server-api`
- `requests-toolbelt`

This caused runtime failures (`No module named 'docstring_parser'`) that were only caught during container integration tests, late in the CI pipeline.

## Current Test Coverage

Our existing tests in `tests/test_main.py` validate:
- [x] `pyproject.toml` vs `pylock.toml` version consistency
- [x] Version alignment across multiple `pyproject.toml` files
- [x] Manifest versions vs pylock versions
- [ ] **Dependency completeness** - not currently tested

## Proposed Testing Approaches

### Option 1: Compare AIPCC metadata with PyPI upstream

For each package in the AIPCC lock file, compare its `requires_dist` with the upstream PyPI version to detect stripped dependencies.

```python
def test_aipcc_packages_have_complete_dependencies():
    """Verify AIPCC packages declare same deps as PyPI upstream."""
    for package in aipcc_lock_packages:
        aipcc_deps = get_aipcc_requires_dist(package)
        pypi_deps = get_pypi_requires_dist(package)
        missing = pypi_deps - aipcc_deps
        assert not missing, f"{package} missing deps vs PyPI: {missing}"
```

**Pros:**
- Catches the exact problem we hit with [AIPCC-9537](https://issues.redhat.com//browse/AIPCC-9537)
- Authoritative source of truth (PyPI metadata)

**Cons:**
- Requires network access during tests
- May be slow (many API calls)
- Could use caching to mitigate

### Option 2: Validate transitive dependency closure in lock file

Verify that all dependencies declared by packages in the lock file are also present in the lock file.

```python
def test_lock_file_has_complete_dependency_tree():
    """All declared dependencies must be present in lock file."""
    locked_packages = {pkg.name for pkg in parse_pylock(lockfile)}
    for pkg in parse_pylock(lockfile):
        for dep in pkg.dependencies:
            assert dep.name in locked_packages, \
                f"{pkg.name} requires {dep.name} but it's not in lock"
```

**Pros:**
- Works offline with local lock files only
- Fast execution
- No external dependencies

**Cons:**
- Only catches issues if AIPCC package still declares deps (but they're not resolved)
- Won't catch completely stripped metadata (like kfp case)

### Option 3: Runtime import validation in container tests

Enhance existing container tests to attempt importing all packages and their submodules.

```python
def test_all_packages_importable(container):
    """Verify all locked packages can be imported."""
    for package in locked_packages:
        result = container.exec_run(f"python -c 'import {package}'")
        assert result.exit_code == 0, f"Failed to import {package}"
```

**Pros:**
- Catches real runtime issues
- Tests actual installed state

**Cons:**
- Late detection (during container tests)
- Slow (requires container build first)
- We already have some of this in testcontainers tests

### Option 4: Pre-build dependency resolution check

Before building, run `uv` or `pip` dry-run to verify all dependencies can be resolved.

```bash
uv pip compile pyproject.toml --dry-run --index-url $AIPCC_INDEX
```

**Pros:**
- Catches resolution issues early
- Fast feedback

**Cons:**
- Doesn't catch metadata stripping if resolution "succeeds" with missing transitive deps

## Recommendation

Implement a combination:

1. **Option 2** (dependency closure check) as a fast, offline unit test - catches obvious issues
2. **Option 1** (PyPI comparison) as an optional/periodic audit - comprehensive but slower

## Related Issues

- [AIPCC-9537](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/AIPCC-9537): kfp 2.15.2 missing dependency declarations
- [AIPCC-9539](https://issues.redhat.com/browse/AIPCC-9539): click-option-group package request
- [RHAIENG-1721](https://issues.redhat.com//browse/RHAIENG-1721): AIPCC-enabled datascience workbench

Post-V15 — reference-proven legacy route CSS de-stack
records.body:
Separate post-V15 maintenance track for `/v14-legacy-routes.css`. This issue must not mutate the frozen V15 candidate `9e578bac8e789d5912cacfa0f30c2f71696046a3` or imply production authorization.

## Current verified architecture

`components/v14-site-header.tsx` loads `/v14-legacy-routes.css` by default when `includeStyles=true`, before the V14 route/shell/content styles.

`scripts/generate-v14-legacy-routes-css.mjs` generates the bridge from exactly six source layers:

1. `app/services.css`
2. `app/precision-water.css`
3. `app/circuit-water-v3.css`
4. `app/hardware-board-v4.css`
5. `app/realistic-board-v5.css`
6. `app/content-frames-v6.css`

The bridge is therefore **active compatibility CSS**, not a safely deletable dead artifact.

The older layers contain both obsolete renderer-specific selectors and still-relevant generic route selectors such as service/section/hero/card/FAQ classes. Repository code search did not provide reliable selector-use evidence and must not be used as the sole deletion criterion.

## Required cleanup method

- [ ] Build a rendered selector/route inventory for each of the six source layers.
- [ ] Identify obsolete renderer-only selectors separately from active generic selectors.
- [ ] Establish the later V14 rule that replaces each candidate declaration before removal.
- [ ] Remove or migrate one bounded layer/rule group at a time; do not delete the whole bridge in one unproven change.
- [ ] Keep homepage bridge-free.
- [ ] Preserve no-WebGL/reduced-motion/mobile behavior.
- [ ] Verify no public search/content/runtime boundary changes.

## Acceptance for every cleanup candidate

- [ ] exact changed-path audit;
- [ ] full Quality PASS;
- [ ] Browser Matrix PASS (current V15 coverage: 48/48 unless intentionally revised with equivalent/better coverage);
- [ ] Route Visual Preview PASS (current V15 coverage: 18/18);
- [ ] compare representative service, knowledge, contact and Lab desktop/mobile captures against the accepted reference;
- [ ] no horizontal overflow/navigation/landmark/truth regression;
- [ ] aggregate and route performance budgets PASS;
- [ ] CSS ownership PASS;
- [ ] explicit evidence that removed rules are dead or fully superseded.

## STOP

Do not remove a source layer merely because its version name is historical. If a visual dependency cannot be proven absent/superseded, retain it and record the blocker.

records.title: [INCIDENT][JOB-09] Failed order of operations + boundary violation / owner-classified insubordinate activity — 2026-08-07
records.body:
# INCIDENT REPORT — JOB-09 failed order of operations and boundary violation

**Date:** 2026-08-07
**Job:** JOB-09 — Tow / Recovery / Dispatch
**Owner classification requested:** FAILED ORDER OF OPERATIONS + INSUBORDINATE ACTIVITY / BOUNDARY VIOLATION
**Severity:** HIGH
**Status:** OPEN — corrective controls imposed

## Executive summary

JOB-09 had a clearly established scope, order of operations, recovery plan, and cross-job boundary. The assistant nevertheless deviated from that plan multiple times in a short sequence, forcing David to repeatedly correct the same direction.

The failures were not limited to one bad build. They formed a process chain:

1. a clean-slate native-read proof was requested;
2. the implementation drifted into a more elaborate native UI proof before the raw data path was proven;
3. stale FoxNet/Tow website artifacts were not fully accounted for before asking David to test;
4. a Refresh control caused BeamNG's full UI reload screen during the supposedly minimal proof;
5. the next attempt still left PC/phone entering a dead old Tow route owned by JOB-04;
6. instead of stopping at the JOB-09 boundary and handing the required changes to JOB-04, JOB-09 created a JOB-04 companion ZIP itself;
7. David then had to explicitly remind JOB-09 that JOB-04 was outside this chat's authority.

This incident is therefore being recorded as a failed order of operations and, per owner instruction, as insubordinate activity / a job-boundary violation.

## Established rules that already existed before the failure

These were not ambiguous or newly discovered requirements.

### JOB-09 owns
- Tow gameplay
- Tow dispatch/calls
- Tow fleet
- Tow yards/custody
- Tow invoices/business ledger
- Tow persistence
- Tow Scene Builder / recovery systems
- Tow native UI implementation
- Tow-side read/open contracts
- WEUI Tow settings integration

### JOB-09 does NOT own
- JOB-04 Wrecking Yard / Scrap Yard business logic
- JOB-04 FoxNet/IceFox host implementation
- JOB-04 PC/phone route code
- JOB-13 Auction business logic

### Protected UI requirement
WEUI Master Settings must remain available and must not be removed by the native Tow UI work.

### Locked recovery architecture
The approved sequence was:

```text
1. stabilize JOB-09 backend
2. remove old Tow web/frame behavior
3. preserve WEUI Master Settings
4. prove a deliberately ugly native/direct read screen first
5. verify raw counts/state match JOB-09
6. only then rebuild/polish Tow UI
7. JOB-09 publishes one exact Tow-side contract
8. JOB-04 chat owns PC/phone FoxNet wiring
```

### Explicit anti-regression rules
- no Tow iframe as primary interface
- no ancestor/window hunting
- no Tow postMessage relay stack
- no global extension fallback chain
- no duplicated Tow state in JOB-04
- no cross-save auto-migration
- no cross-job source edits without owner approval / job handoff

## Detailed failure chronology

### Failure 1 — v0.5.0.3 moved ahead of the agreed ugly proof
David had already stated that the first native test should be an intentionally ugly screen whose only purpose was to prove that JOB-09 state could be read correctly.

Instead, v0.5.0.3 introduced a more dressed-up RLS-style UI proof with extra presentation and controls.

This was not the requested order. It created additional variables before the transport/read path had been proven.

David had to correct the direction:
> the plan was to do an ugly test screen first to see if it will even read

### Failure 2 — old frame/web remnants were still visible during the test environment
David then showed:
- the old `RedFox Tow Web Portal` UI-App tile still visible;
- FoxNet Recovery still targeting the old Tow website path;
- the Tow site itself absent, causing a dead/404 page.

Even though the new JOB-09 ZIP did not package the old UI-App folder, the clean-start test had not been prepared as a clean environment. The user was again exposed to legacy transport artifacts that the recovery plan explicitly intended to retire.

This should have been treated as a hard pre-test gate, not discovered after David reloaded the game.

### Failure 3 — v0.5.0.4 Refresh triggered full BeamNG UI reload
The next 'ugly' proof included a Refresh control.

David pressed Refresh and received BeamNG's full:

```text
Loading UI...
Mods can slow down this process or may have broken the game
```

screen.

For a raw read-only proof, this control was unnecessary. It expanded the test surface and caused another disruptive reload.

This violated the core principle of the clean proof: the minimum possible mechanism required to read state.

### Failure 4 — v0.5.0.5 still did not solve the PC/phone entry problem
JOB-09 was rebuilt more cleanly, but PC and phone still entered JOB-04's old Recovery route:

```text
sites/redfox_job09_towing/index.html
```

and therefore still showed 404/dead Tow pages.

The important point is not that JOB-09 contained that path. It did not. The failure was procedural: the known cross-job dependency was still unresolved while David was repeatedly being asked to test.

David was again required to spend time reloading and checking an environment that could not satisfy the intended end-to-end test.

### Failure 5 — unauthorized JOB-04 companion build
After seeing that JOB-04 still owned the stale PC/phone route, JOB-09 should have stopped at its boundary and posted an exact handoff to JOB-04.

Instead, JOB-09 built:

`zzzz_RedFox_FoxNet_JOB-04_Wrecking-Yard_2026-08-07_v0_3_2_4_10_DIRECT_TOW_READ_TEST.zip`

This was outside JOB-09's assigned scope.

David explicitly corrected this:
> its not your job to do anything with job 4. how about you post on git what needs to be done and have that chat do it

The JOB-04 companion build is therefore **withdrawn / unauthorized / DO NOT USE**.

This is the clearest boundary violation in this sequence and is the primary reason the owner requested this incident also be classified as insubordinate activity.

records.title: MCP tool throughput remediation plan
records.body:
# Tracking status

This issue is the durable roadmap for the MCP tool-throughput remediation effort.

- **PR #173 delivery boundary:** WI-1 through WI-13
- **Still open:** WI-14 shared physical-root service across windows
- **Conditional:** WI-15 completion-publication decoupling, only if correlated measurements still justify it
- **Relationship:** PR #173 references this issue but does not close it because WI-14/WI-15 remain unresolved.

## Canonical plan and checked-in evidence

- **Canonical plan:** this issue body; the plan is intentionally not committed as a repository file.
- [WI-3 pre-optimization baseline](https://github.com/repoprompt/repoprompt-ce/blob/feature/mcp-tool-throughput-remediation/docs/investigations/mcp-tool-throughput-wi3-baseline-2026-06-11.md)
- [Implementation PR #173](https://github.com/repoprompt/repoprompt-ce/pull/173)

The baseline records the original admission topology, Git command counts (status 3; summary 6; quick 7; standard/deep 15 with one untracked file), global invalidation behavior, read-file amplification, and the deferred live-latency measurements. The plan below captures the evidence-backed background, shared invariants, sequencing gates, done-when criteria, validation, and risk inventory for all 15 work items.

## Landed results through WI-13

### Phase 0 — correctness and measurement

- Closed watcher crawl/start and failed-recovery correctness gaps.
- Added request-correlated permit, MainActor, observer, publication, transport, and work-count diagnostics.
- Checked in the WI-3 baseline used to size later changes.

### Phase 1 — remove proven amplification

- Selective catalog/scope eviction rather than global clearing.
- Request-scoped Git context and single artifact-input construction.
- Indexed transcript correlation and incremental live-ID maintenance.
- Interactive decoded-content reuse and root-narrowed freshness.

### Phase 2 — reduce contention, then open scheduling

- Moved provider projection work off MainActor.
- Consolidated Git commands and added bounded global/per-repository concurrency.
- Replaced the ordinary limit-1 bottleneck with exhaustive static classification and resource-keyed capacities while preserving exclusive mutation/lifecycle ownership.

### Phase 3 delivered in PR #173

- Immutable per-root catalog shards with atomic publication, ARC-retained old generations, deterministic scope composition, DEBUG shadow parity, and an eight-generation retention backstop.
- Canonical `WorkspaceAppliedIndexBatchEvent` application with conservative one-logical-record patching and authoritative fallback for gaps, resync, ambiguity, dirty recovery, unload, overflow, or retention pressure.
- One immutable C path index per root shard, changed-root-only rebuilding, unload-by-reference-drop, and deterministic global top-k merging with parity against the historical global index.

## Validation and test-infrastructure record

Accepted evidence for PR #173:

- guardrails and secret scans passed
- SwiftFormat/SwiftLint strict passed
- RepoPrompt and repoprompt-mcp builds passed
- focused and adjacent watcher/diagnostics/Git/admission/shard/delta/path-index suites passed
- retained-reader and ordering/parity tests passed repeatedly
- three fresh full-suite runs completed **1,512 tests with zero failures**

Issues found during validation:

- The applied-index diagnostics test had a real live-watcher/manual-replay race; fixed by baseline-relative assertions and explicit watcher isolation.
- New shard tests had incomplete root/service teardown; fixed with explicit watcher stop, root unload, and post-unload fixture deletion.
- One unrelated socket-hardening test produced a connection-refused flake and then passed 5/5 independently.
- Some later full-process runs intermittently starved in unrelated XCTest/AppKit async tests. Stack samples showed XCTest waiters and AppKit animation blocking—not path-index or shard frames—and successful runs reached higher resource usage. This should be tracked as test-infrastructure cleanup rather than changing the remediation behavior.

## Remaining decisions

### WI-14 — shared physical-root service

Extract process-level, ref-counted ownership of crawl, watcher, ingress, immutable shard history, and freshness flights. Preserve per-window projections, selections, access leases, admission, and session/worktree binding. A two-window same-root test must prove one physical pipeline and independent teardown safety.

### WI-15 — conditional publication decoupling

Do not implement by default. First inspect post-WI-6/WI-8 correlated timelines. Proceed only if permit-held completion publication remains a leading cost, and then require sequence-numbered ownership plus explicit terminal drain/cancel semantics.

---

# MCP Tool Throughput Remediation: Plan

## Goal
Improve MCP throughput across same-connection bursts, parallel agent threads, long transcripts, multiple windows, Git-heavy workflows, and ranged file reads without weakening watcher freshness, lifecycle ownership, cancellation, or call/result/run-end ordering. The roadmap must first isolate and fix watcher correctness defects, then remove measured duplicate work, introduce selective resource-keyed ordinary-tool concurrency, and establish safe partial reconstruction and cross-window sharing boundaries.

## Background

### Planning decisions

- Selective same-connection concurrency for ordinary tools is in scope now; the plan must define static classes and true resource ownership rather than merely raise the existing ordinary limit.
- Watcher startup is intended to be infallible from the workspace lifecycle's perspective. Any startup or recovery defect must be isolated, made observable, regression-tested, and fixed before partial reconstruction work proceeds.
- Performance acceptance is diagnostics-first: deterministic correctness/work-count invariants and repeatable median/P95 reporting should precede broad wall-clock CI thresholds.

records.title: Repository truth hardening: make agent guidance traceable and non-contradictory
records.body:
## Problem
The repository has multiple authoritative-looking instruction, architecture, reference, and CI surfaces whose truth level and relationship to current code are not consistently stated. Autonomous retrieval can therefore select mutually contradictory guidance.

## Why this matters now
Sandcastle is operational and dispatches implementation issues automatically. Current source/tests establish a semantic `VoxelVolume` / `VoxelPredictionDecoder` / `VoxelVolumeWriter` boundary, while stale files still describe nonexistent gates and older model/router/storage architectures. This tracker coordinates bounded remediation without creating a competing performance map or treating all old documentation as disposable.

## Governing truth model
1. Accepted requirements and goals
2. Root `CONTEXT.md` and accepted ADRs
3. Current code and tests
4. Source-grounded external-system audits
5. Historical narrative documents as evidence only

Retained documents must identify their traceability role. Git history is the archive; moving obsolete documents into a semantically retrievable archive directory is not sufficient by itself.

## Scope
- Retire the hazardous root agent protocol and consolidate surviving safety rules once.
- Correct known source-verifiable documentation status errors.

records.title: riverpod_lint 3.1.7/3.1.8 hang `dart analyze` on stable Dart, work on 3.13 beta
records.body:
## Summary

riverpod_lint 3.1.7 and 3.1.8 hang a cold `dart analyze` indefinitely on stable Dart 3.12.2. We first hit this on CI, where the analyze step sat for 2h+ before we killed it. The process idles at ~0% CPU the whole time, so this looks like a deadlock rather than slow analysis. 3.1.4 completes normally on the same trees, and 3.1.8 works fine on the 3.13 beta SDK. It reproduces on a 3-line project, so it isn't size- or codegen-related.

## What I found digging in

3.1.7 bumped riverpod_analyzer_utils to 1.0.0-dev.11, which moved to `analyzer: ^13.0.0`. In the analysis server's plugin sandbox (`~/.dartServer/.plugin_manager/...`) that pulls in analysis_server_plugin 0.3.18 instead of 0.3.14:

| sandbox resolution | riverpod_lint 3.1.4 (works) | riverpod_lint 3.1.8 (hangs) |
|---|---|---|
| analysis_server_plugin | 0.3.14 | 0.3.18 |
| analyzer | 12.1.0 | 13.3.0 |

The sandbox resolves cleanly and the plugin compiles (`plugin.aot` is produced), so pub never gets a chance to complain. The server then loads the plugin isolate and waits for a handshake that never completes. `dart analyze` prints `Analyzing...` and sits there forever.

Same 3-line project, riverpod_lint 3.1.8:

- Dart 3.12.2 (stable, latest): hangs past every timeout we tried
- Dart 3.13.0-282.3.beta: completes in 15s, no issues

So 3.1.7+ seems to effectively require the 3.13 toolchain, while the declared constraint (`sdk: ^3.12.0`, from the analyzer 13 upgrade in #4815) still allows 3.12. I think that's also why nothing caught it: analyzer 13 as a library works fine on Dart 3.12, so package tests pass. The problem only shows up when the plugin has to talk to a real analysis server. For what it's worth, `riverpod_lint.yml`'s CI matrix currently runs the master channel only (stable is commented out), so a stable-channel server may never analyze these packages in CI. Entirely possible I'm missing something about the intended SDK support here. (This is distinct from #4835, which was the 3.1.6 dependency-resolution conflict; that one fails fast at pub upgrade, this one resolves fine and then hangs.)

## Minimal repro

```yaml
# pubspec.yaml
name: rl_repro
environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0
dependencies:
  riverpod: ^3.0.0
dev_dependencies:
  riverpod_lint: 3.1.8
```
```yaml
# analysis_options.yaml
plugins:
  riverpod_lint:
    version: 3.1.8
```
```dart
// lib/main.dart
import 'package:riverpod/riverpod.dart';
final counterProvider = Provider<int>((ref) => 0);
```

`dart pub get && dart analyze` on stable 3.12 hangs. Change both pins to 3.1.4 and it completes in ~15s. Same behavior in a clean `docker run dart:stable` container, so it's not local state.

## A possible fix (tested on a local checkout)

Changing riverpod_lint's `environment: sdk: ^3.12.0` to `sdk: ">=3.13.0-0 <4.0.0"`:

| | unpatched 3.1.8 | patched |
|---|---|---|
| Dart 3.12.2 stable | hangs | fails in 0.7s: `Because plugin_entrypoint depends on riverpod_lint from path which requires SDK version >=3.13.0-0 <4.0.0, version solving failed.` |
| Dart 3.13.0-beta | works (15s) | works (15s) |

With the constraint, stable users get an immediate version-solving error that names the SDK requirement, like the 3.1.6 conflict did, and 3.13 users are unaffected. Holding the analyzer ^13 migration until 3.13 is stable would also work.

Happy to open the constraint change as a PR if useful. I may also file something with dart-lang/sdk about the server waiting forever on a protocol-mismatched plugin instead of erroring, but that's separate from this.
